What Strata Management Actually Runs

About 1.5 million people live in British Columbia strata housing, across residential, commercial and mixed-use buildings, as well as townhouses, duplexes and bare-land developments. Each property type creates a different set of shared operating needs.

A townhouse owner who finds water staining on a hallway ceiling can report it, but resolving the problem may involve shared pipes, insurance, a maintenance budget and a contractor. The corporation's governance and operating arrangements determine how common-property work is investigated and authorized.

Owners hold title to their individual strata lots, while the corporation manages shared property and assets. Council members carry out the corporation's work under the Strata Property Act, its regulations, bylaws and rules. A vote can authorize a decision where required, but it does not change who owns a shared pipe or make every operational duty a contractor's responsibility.
One legal framework, very different workloads

A four-unit bare-land site and a high-rise may both be strata corporations, yet their vendor needs, maintenance plans and utility controls can differ. A tower may require coordinated inspections of elevators and mechanical systems. A smaller development may have fewer shared systems, while still needing clear responsibility for roads, drainage or common water use.
Strata management turns shared ownership into ongoing work: organizing repairs, tracking common expenses, keeping records, communicating with residents and planning for future capital needs.
Multifamily property management and shared building operations
offers a useful starting point for understanding these duties, which must then be matched to the corporation's own assets and rules.

For a council, the practical questions are who can approve each decision, what supports the budget, and how utility charges fit the bylaws. Clear answers help the corporation handle routine operations as well as unexpected bills, leaks and repairs.
Who May Decide and Who Only Advises
People often use “the strata” to mean the owners, the council, the property manager and the service providers all at once. That shorthand hides an important distinction:
doing administrative work isn't the same as holding decision-making authority
. The table below shows the usual division of responsibility. The Act, the corporation's bylaws and resolutions, and the terms of each contract determine the exact limits.
Party
Typically decides
Everyday example
Cannot do
Owners at a general meeting
Bylaws, budgets and major spending set by the Act
Approve the annual budget and a special levy
Run day-to-day repairs between meetings
Elected strata council
Operations within bylaws and owner resolutions
Instruct a roof tender and set council meeting agendas
Change a bylaw without the required vote
Professional strata manager
Contracted administration and vendor coordination
Issue notices, code invoices and chase quotes
Spend past the delegated limit or set strata fees
Self-managed directors
Both governance and the daily operating load
Make council decisions and handle manager paperwork
Treat volunteer status as a lower legal duty
Specialist contractor
The scoped trade or engineering task
Replace a pump or prepare a depreciation report
Set contribution rates or enforce bylaws
Submetering provider
Reads, billing and meter upkeep under the agreement
Invoice suite use and report common-area load
Amend bylaws or decide the strata fee
Delegation has boundaries

A professional manager works within a contract and any spending authority the corporation has delegated. The agreement may assign notices, vendor coordination and invoice coding, but it doesn't transfer the corporation's responsibility for maintaining common property or adopting a lawful budget. If the manager can approve emergency work up to a stated limit, they may be able to dispatch a plumber for a burst pipe. That doesn't mean they can award a major façade contract without the necessary approval.

A submetering agreement can assign meter ownership during the term, readings, monthly billing and resident questions. It can't authorise a charge that the bylaws or applicable rules don't permit, change fee levels set through the corporation's process or approve capital spending. Meter data is evidence about consumption, not a substitute for governance authority.

Specialists have a different boundary. An engineer can assess a system and recommend a repair, while a contractor can perform the work in the agreed scope. Neither one sets owner contributions or enforces bylaws by virtue of being hired.
Before the next meeting, write one accountable name beside each of these: the budget, insurance renewal, common-area utilities and emergency repairs.
If a duty has no named owner, a contract or a committee title may not be enough to get it done.
Duties That Stay with the Council
Ontario's Condominium Authority reported that
2,203 condominium corporations were self-managed in 2024–2025
, with directors rather than professional managers overseeing daily operations in those corporations (
Condominium Authority of Ontario annual report
). The figure is from Ontario, but the operational question is familiar to volunteer boards everywhere: who checks the bills, coordinates the work and notices an exception?
Start with a monthly utility-control routine. It gives a self-managed council a practical way to spot an unusual charge or consumption pattern before it becomes a longer dispute.
Compare the master bill.
Check it against the same period in the prior year and consider whether seasonal use, such as irrigation or heating, explains the difference.
Separate shared and suite use.
Confirm what the bill covers. If the master meter combines common-area demand with unit-level consumption, don't treat the total as a clean measure of either.
Record exceptions.
Log a suspected meter issue, billing discrepancy or unusual reading with its date and affected area or unit. Keep the bill and related correspondence with the record.
Name the accountable party.
Decide whether the next action belongs to the corporation, manager, utility provider or contractor. “Someone should call” isn't an assignment.
Escalate repeated variance.
If the pattern persists, follow up before the corporation faces a larger budget impact, property damage or an owner dispute.
Self-managed doesn't mean low complexity. It can shift hidden administrative and compliance work onto unpaid directors.
Make the handoffs visible

Self-management doesn't shrink the council's core workload. The board still needs to arrange lawful meetings, keep records, place insurance, enforce bylaws, adopt a budget and maintain common property. Directors also need a process for vendor oversight, billing checks and service interruptions. For another operational checklist,
property security responsibilities for strata managers
can help a board identify where security-related duties need a clear owner.

Ask prospective utility or maintenance vendors specific questions: What does the scope include? How often will readings or inspections occur? What service level applies when an issue is reported? How are disputed charges handled? What are the agreement's exit terms, and what data or equipment handoff follows?

For a disputed charge or service interruption, record the event, pull the last twelve months of master-meter data, notify owners in writing and escalate to the utility provider or contractor within a response window set by the board. The council should also state who confirms receipt and who reports back. If nobody can say who validates the water bill this month, that duty is unassigned, even if the bylaws are tidy.
How the Annual Budget Gets Its Numbers
A budget is only as useful as the assumptions behind it. In British Columbia, strata corporations with
five or more strata lots must obtain a depreciation report every five years
. The report inventories and evaluates common-property components, estimates their remaining useful lives and repair or replacement costs, and supports a
30-year funding forecast
, according to the
provincial depreciation-report requirements

The report should help a council connect the condition of assets to annual contingency-reserve contributions. Its financial section sets out assumptions for inflation and investment interest and compares at least three funding models. Before adopting a budget, reconcile the preferred model with the current contingency-reserve balance and any approved projects that haven't yet been paid for.
Model
How money is raised
What owners feel
Risk left behind
Steady contingency contributions
Annual contributions sized to the 30-year forecast
Higher but predictable strata fees
Underfunding if inflation assumptions are too soft
Special levies
One-time charges when a project is approved
Sudden large bills
Hardest on fixed incomes and slow to collect
Increased strata fees
Capital loaded into the operating fee
A visible monthly increase
Operating and capital costs can become unclear if not labelled
Borrowing
A loan repaid over later years
Interest and repayment on top of fees
Debt service can crowd out the next repair
Blended model
Reserve, levy and loan in combination
Costs shared across current and future owners
Harder to explain clearly at the meeting
Make the trade-off understandable

Take a roof approaching replacement. Higher reserve contributions spread funding through regular budgets, but owners pay more before the work begins. A special levy may avoid carrying a loan, but it can require owners to find a large amount at once. Borrowing shifts payments into later years and adds debt service to future costs. A blended approach can spread the pressure, but council should explain who pays when and why.

A low contribution rate isn't a saving. It leaves a funding gap that may later require a levy or loan, especially if a roof, elevator, façade, domestic-water system or mechanical plant fails before the reserve can cover the work. Deferring a project can also mean emergency procurement, consequential damage or service disruption.

The annual package should let owners follow the reasoning without guessing. Include the assumption page, the comparison between funding models and a clear line from this year's contribution to the forecast's remaining gap. A consistent record also helps when a treasurer needs to
manage rental accounts with QuickBooks
, particularly where the corporation or its agents handle multiple accounts and supporting records.
For utility-related costs, councils can also review
energy management system approaches
alongside the building's broader budget. The important distinction is to show which amounts fund routine operations and which build the reserve for future work.
Turning Condition Reports into Work Orders
A useful maintenance plan separates
recurring operating work
from
contingency-reserve projects

and connects both to documented asset condition. In British Columbia, the depreciation report's required structure includes a physical component inventory and evaluation, non-annual maintenance and repair work, projected costs, funding assumptions, and the reserve's current balance and funding sources (
the Land Title and Survey Authority's depreciation-report guidance
). That information should lead to inspections and work orders, not sit unused in a report.
Build an asset register people can act on

For each major component, keep its location, installation date, expected life, inspection history, condition score, replacement estimate and responsible party. The manager or treasurer should be able to see what was last checked, what needs attention next and which budget line supports the work. Update the forecast when an inspection, tender or failure changes a material assumption.

A domestic-water riser may deserve earlier attention than a cosmetic item with a similar average annual replacement cost. If the riser has little remaining life and a failure could damage multiple areas, the consequence of waiting is greater. Risk-based planning looks at
failure consequence, remaining life and replacement cost
, not just the annualised figure.
Turn condition into a planned job

Once the council identifies a project, define the scope, record the condition evidence and schedule procurement while the system is still working. Tendering before failure gives bidders a clearer scope and the corporation more opportunity to compare offers. A failed elevator or flooded mechanical room can force emergency rates and disrupt services while the council and contractor decide what must be done first.
Regular inspection is part of that discipline. A practical
rental property inspection checklist
can prompt useful questions about what to document, although the strata's inspection scope should reflect its own common property and specialist advice.

Owners can better understand a fee change when the minutes connect it to a condition score, estimated replacement cost and chosen schedule. A documented asset record makes the case easier to follow than a surprise invoice with no visible path from inspection to budget.
Two Buildings and Two Operating Loads
On Monday night, the treasurer of a
12-lot townhouse

sits down with the master water bill. The corporation has no professional manager, and the bill covers both irrigation and suites. A boiler has failed, and because old condition notes never became reserve contributions, the council is discussing a special levy. Before the meeting ends, the treasurer has also chased two owners for unpaid fees and called a plumber, without a written delegated spending limit to guide the call.

The problem isn't that a small site should have the same management structure as a tower. It's that the board still needs a named person to check the water bill, keep track of the boiler's condition and know who can authorise urgent work. A short list of shared assets can still create a complicated evening when responsibilities aren't assigned.
A tower needs clean data too
Now consider a
180-lot high-rise

with a manager and a current depreciation report. Common-area electricity is metered separately from suite use, and a leak alert from a riser reaches the manager before water spreads through the building. The council's meeting is about approving a tender, not cleaning up unclear utility records.

That arrangement brings more systems and coordination work, but it doesn't remove the need for a bylaw basis before occupants are billed. Accurate readings can show what happened; they don't decide who is legally responsible for a charge.

Commercial or mixed-use properties add another wrinkle. A ground-floor unit may have different hours and loads from residential suites, so the council shouldn't average its use into a residential fee without a measured split and a sound authority to charge. The small site has fewer components, the tower has more systems, and both need an accountable person for each task.
Which building does your corporation resemble this quarter?
Fitting Submetering into Bylaws and Decisions
Before a strata considers occupant utility billing, it needs a
bylaw and local-rules check

. A meter can record use, but it can't create authority to charge residents. The council should also keep common-property consumption with the corporation rather than treating shared loads as if they belonged to individual suites.
Posture
Question the council asks
Data required
Limit
Billing-first
Who should pay for measured use?
Suite use separated from common-area use
Occupant charges must be allowed by bylaws and local rules
Resilience-first
What is leaking, flooding or spiking?
Baselines, leak alerts and shutoff points
Visibility alone doesn't authorise a charge
Shared strata fees
Leave utilities inside the monthly fee
Master-meter total and an allocation method
Hides suite waste and can slow leak detection
The resilience case isn't just about recovering costs. British Columbia's
2025 climate-risk assessment
identifies riverine and coastal flooding, extreme heat, wildfire, drought or water scarcity, and earthquakes among the province's priority hazards (
the provincial climate-risk assessment
). Consumption baselines and leak alerts can give a council, insurer or engineer a clearer record of what changed and where to investigate. They're evidence for decisions, not a promise of savings.
Use this four-part check before choosing equipment or billing arrangements:
Read the bylaws for authority to recover utility use and identify which loads remain common property.
Confirm the provincial or municipal rules before billing occupants.
Define the problem, whether it's allocation fairness, unexplained common-area costs or leaks that go unnoticed.
Scope the meters, readings and billing only after the first three points are clear.

If the authority check fails, address it before proceeding. If authority is sound but the corporation can't distinguish suite use from common-area demand, request a property and jurisdiction assessment before setting the scope. For more on the billing side of that decision, see
how to bill tenants for utilities
